title: Interrupts, exceptions and signals
summary: How a running program gets interrupted: hardware interrupts, CPU exceptions (traps, faults, aborts) and Unix signals, the common signals and their default actions, suspending and resuming with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT, installing a signal handler from Rust with an atomic flag, what is allowed inside a handler, why setjmp and longjmp do not fit Rust, and the graceful-shutdown pattern.

RiA 12.5.4 Handling signals with custom actions
RiA 12.5.5 Using a global variable to indicate that shutdown has been initiated
RiA 12.6.1 Understanding function pointers and their syntax
RiA 12.8 Shutting down from deeply nested call stacks

blocks.md: A program does not run uninterrupted. The keyboard, the network card and the timer all need the CPU's attention; a program can divide by zero or touch memory it does not own; the user can press Ctrl-C. *Rust in Action*'s last chapter sorts these events into three kinds and follows each one from the hardware to your code.

blocks.title: Three ways to interrupt a program
rows: key pressed, packet arrived, timer tick
the CPU, caused by the current instruction
the kernel; may become a signal
divide by zero, page fault, invalid instruction, breakpoint
the process: a default action or your handler
SIGINT from Ctrl-C, SIGSEGV after a bad pointer, SIGTERM from kill

blocks.md: Exceptions come in three flavors. A **trap** is deliberate, like a breakpoint or a system call; execution continues after it. A **fault** can be fixed and the instruction retried, like a page fault that loads memory from swap. An **abort** cannot be recovered. When the kernel cannot fix a fault on the program's behalf (the address really is invalid), it turns it into a **signal**, such as `SIGSEGV`, and delivers it to the process. Signals are the Unix way for the kernel to tell a process "something happened to you".

blocks.title: What happens when you press Ctrl-C

steps.title: The keyboard raises an interrupt
steps.md: The keyboard controller signals the CPU. The CPU stops the current instruction stream and jumps to the kernel's interrupt handler, registered in the interrupt descriptor table.
steps.code: CPU running your program ──► keyboard IRQ ──► kernel interrupt handler

steps.title: The terminal driver sees Ctrl-C
steps.md: The kernel's terminal (tty) driver recognizes the interrupt character and, instead of passing `^C` as input, sends **SIGINT** to the foreground process group.
steps.code: tty driver: ^C  ──►  kill(foreground process group, SIGINT)

steps.title: The signal is marked pending
steps.md: The kernel sets a pending bit for SIGINT on the process. If the process has SIGINT blocked, the bit just waits.

steps.title: Delivery on the way back to user space
steps.md: The next time the process returns from the kernel to user space, the kernel checks pending, unblocked signals. With no handler, the default action for SIGINT runs: terminate. With a handler, the kernel arranges for your function to run first, then resumes the program where it was.
steps.code:
default:  process terminated by signal 2
handler:  on_interrupt(2) runs, then the program continues

blocks.title: Common signals on Linux
rows: `abort()`, which Rust uses for some fatal errors
integer divide by zero in C (Rust checks and panics first)
`kill -9`; cannot be caught, blocked or ignored
writing to a closed pipe (Rust ignores it at startup)
`kill`, a polite request to shut down

blocks.title: Suspending and resuming
blocks.md: `SIGSTOP` freezes a process and `SIGCONT` resumes it, which is how shells implement job control. *Rust in Action* demonstrates it from a shell (the numbers are Linux's; macOS numbers some signals differently, so prefer the names):

blocks.code:
$ sleep 60 &
[1] 2873
$ kill -STOP 2873      # or kill -SIGSTOP %1
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 60
$ kill -CONT 2873
$ kill -TERM 2873
[1]+  Terminated              sleep 60
$ kill -l              # list every signal name and number
blocks.explain: Numbers and job ids will differ on your machine. Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, the catchable cousin of SIGSTOP; `fg` and `bg` send SIGCONT.

blocks.title: Handling a signal in Rust
blocks.md:
The C function **`signal(sig, handler)`** installs a handler, and **`raise(sig)`** sends a signal to the current process, which lets a program test its own handling. Real code takes these and the signal numbers from the **`libc`** crate, as *Rust in Action* does; here they are declared by hand, as in lesson 1, and the numbers are Linux's.

A handler can run **between any two instructions** of your program, even while `main` holds a lock or is halfway through `malloc`. So it may only do things that are **async-signal-safe**: no `println!`, no allocation, no locks. The safe pattern is to set a flag and let the main loop act on it. *Rust in Action* used a `static mut bool`; since the 2024 edition, references to a `static mut` are an error, and the correct tool is an **atomic**, which is lock-free and safe to touch from a handler.

blocks.output: stopped after 10 iterations, SIGUSR1 seen 3 times
blocks.explain: Without the SIGTERM handler, `raise(SIGTERM)` would end the process on the spot, skipping every destructor. With it, the loop notices the flag and leaves normally, so cleanup code runs. The handlers are `extern "C" fn`s because the kernel calls them with the C convention; *Rust in Action* shows that a function pointer is just an address by printing `handle_sigterm as usize`.

blocks.title: Things not to do in a signal handler
blocks.md: Do not print, allocate, lock a `Mutex`, or call most library functions: if the signal arrived while the main code held the same lock or was inside the allocator, the handler deadlocks or corrupts it. Do not panic either: the handler is an `extern "C"` function, so a panic aborts. Store to an atomic, write a byte to a pipe, or call one of the few functions POSIX lists as async-signal-safe.

blocks.title: Escaping from deep call stacks
blocks.md:
*Rust in Action* also shows C's **`setjmp` / `longjmp`**: `setjmp` saves the CPU registers, and a later `longjmp` jumps straight back to that point from anywhere deeper in the call stack, as if `setjmp` had returned again. It works through LLVM intrinsics and nightly Rust, and the book warns that it is dangerous. In Rust it is worse than dangerous: jumping over stack frames **skips their destructors**, so locks stay locked and memory leaks, and it is undefined behavior if any skipped frame had something to drop.

Use Rust's own tools instead: return a `Result` and let `?` carry it up, or, for truly exceptional cases, panic and `catch_unwind` at a boundary (lesson 1). Both run every destructor on the way.

blocks.title: Graceful shutdown in practice
blocks.md:
Production programs rarely call `signal` themselves:

- The **`signal-hook`** crate installs handlers correctly (with `sigaction`), offers flags (`signal_hook::flag::register(SIGTERM, Arc::clone(&term))`) and an iterator of incoming signals you can read from a normal thread, where printing and locking are allowed.
- The **`ctrlc`** crate handles Ctrl-C on both Unix and Windows. Windows has no signals; it has console control events, which `ctrlc` maps to the same callback.
- Async runtimes have `tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await`, which fits the cancellation model from chapter 17.

The design is always the one above: the handler only **records** that a shutdown was requested; the main loop or a dedicated thread **acts** on it by finishing current work, closing connections and flushing files. Chapter 25's web server shuts down this way.

blocks.title: Survive Ctrl-C
blocks.md: The program pretends the user pressed Ctrl-C after job 3 by raising SIGINT. Right now nothing handles it, so the process dies before cleaning up. Install `on_interrupt` for SIGINT and make it set `STOP`, so the loop ends and the cleanup line runs.
blocks.task: Print `job 1 done`, `job 2 done`, `job 3 done`, `cleaning up and exiting`.
blocks.expected_output:
job 1 done
job 2 done
job 3 done
cleaning up and exiting
hints: In the handler: `STOP.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);` and nothing else.

blocks.title: A model of signal delivery
blocks.goal: Model how the kernel delivers signals to a process: default actions, handlers, ignoring, blocking with a bit mask, pending signals, and the two signals nobody can catch.
blocks.behavior:
Signals are numbered as on Linux. This is a simplified model: a signal that is not blocked is delivered at once, even to a stopped process.
- `pub fn from_number(n: i32) -> Option<Signal>` and `pub fn default_action(s: Signal) -> Action` following the table in the lesson (HUP, INT, KILL, USR1, USR2, PIPE, ALRM, TERM terminate; QUIT, ILL, ABRT, FPE, SEGV dump core; CHLD is ignored; STOP and TSTP stop; CONT continues).
- `Process::new()`: alive, not stopped, every disposition `Default`, nothing blocked or pending.
- `set_disposition(s, d) -> Result<(), &'static str>`: an `Err` for `Kill` and `Stop`, which cannot be caught or ignored.
- `block(s)` / `unblock(s) -> Option<Outcome>` and `blocked_mask() -> u32` (bit `n` for signal number `n`). `Kill` and `Stop` cannot be blocked: `block` does nothing for them. `unblock` delivers the signal if it was pending.
- `send(s) -> Outcome`: `NoProcess` once the process has died. If `s` is blocked, mark it pending and return `Pending` (a second one while pending merges with the first: standard signals do not queue). Otherwise deliver it:
  - `Cont` always resumes a stopped process, then returns `Handled(Cont)` if it has a handler and `Continued` otherwise.
  - `Ignore` gives `Ignored`; `Handle` records the signal in `handled()` and gives `Handled(s)`.
  - `Default` follows `default_action`: `Terminated(s)` or `CoreDumped(s)` (and the process is dead), `Ignored`, or `Stopped`.
- `is_alive()`, `is_stopped()`, `is_pending(s)`, `handled() -> &[Signal]`.

examples.input: block(Usr1) with a handler, send(Usr1) twice, then unblock(Usr1)
examples.output: Pending, Pending, then Some(Handled(Usr1)), and handled() == [Usr1]

hints: `from_number` is one `match` with a `_ => None` arm.
Index `dispositions` with `s as usize`; the bit for a signal is `1u32 << (s as u32)`.
Write a private `deliver(&mut self, s) -> Outcome` and call it from both `send` and `unblock`.
blocks.solution_explain: The kernel really does keep two bit masks per thread, blocked and pending, which is why a second SIGUSR1 sent while the first is pending is lost: a bit cannot count. Putting delivery in one private `deliver` method keeps `send` and `unblock` consistent. Kill and Stop are refused in both `set_disposition` and `block`, so no process can make itself unkillable.

questions.q: Which of these comes from the current instruction rather than a device?
questions.explanation: Exceptions are caused by the instruction being executed.

questions.q: Which two signals can never be caught, blocked or ignored?
questions.explanation: So the system can always stop or kill a process.

questions.q: What should a signal handler do?
options: Set an atomic flag and return
Lock a Mutex and update state
questions.explanation: Only async-signal-safe work; the main loop acts on the flag.

questions.q: Why is `longjmp` a bad fit for Rust?
options: It skips the destructors of the frames it jumps over

questions.q: SIGUSR1 is blocked and sent three times. How many times does its handler run after unblocking?
questions.explanation: Standard signals set one pending bit; they do not queue.

points: Hardware interrupts come from devices, exceptions from the current instruction, signals from the kernel to a process.
Each signal has a default action: terminate, core dump, ignore, stop or continue.
SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.
Handlers run between any two instructions, so they only set atomics or do other async-signal-safe work.
Blocked signals wait as pending bits and do not queue.
Graceful shutdown: the handler records the request, the main loop acts on it; use signal-hook or ctrlc in real code.

terms.def: A signal from hardware that makes the CPU stop and run a handler in the kernel.
An event caused by the current CPU instruction: a trap, a fault or an abort.
A notification the kernel delivers to a process, such as SIGINT or SIGTERM.
A function the kernel runs in the process when a signal is delivered.
Safe to call from a signal handler, even if the signal interrupted the same code.
A signal that has been sent but not yet delivered, usually because it is blocked.
